meta.title: N1 news lens: three worked stories, a units spotter and the evidence ladder
meta.note: Headlines are paraphrased in our own words; no outlet is quoted. Facts come from the primary sources linked, as of the dates given (all checked 2026-11-02). Story 3's early single-cause claims are described, not dated. Spotter sentences are illustrative composites; where they use a real number, its source is named. Toy durations and utilization rates are labeled illustrative.

lens.label: Scale
lens.ask: How big is it next to the whole?
lens.trap: A big-sounding number that is a small share, or a national figure read as a global one.

lens.label: Time
lens.ask: Power or energy? Which hour, which year?
lens.trap: GW read as GWh, or a 2030 projection read as today's fact.

lens.label: Physics
lens.ask: Do the units, losses and limits make sense?
lens.trap: Nameplate (the maximum rated power) treated as typical output, or a unit that cannot be right.

lens.label: Who pays
lens.ask: Who pays, who benefits, who carries the risk?
lens.trap: Savings for one group that other customers end up paying for.

lens.label: Boundary
lens.ask: What is counted, and what is left out?
lens.trap: A total that quietly leaves out part of the system.

lens.label: Counterfactual
lens.trap: A change measured against a baseline that would never have happened.

lens.label: Uncertainty
lens.ask: How sure, says who, with what range?
lens.trap: One number from one party, with no range.

stories.kicker: Data centers as a load · United States
stories.headline: U.S. data centers could use nearly 12% of the nation's electricity by 2030
stories.framing: Our paraphrase of how such reports get headlined.
parts: A national-laboratory report estimates that data centers used

parts.note: Energy over a whole year, not power. Spread over 2024's 8,784 hours (a leap year) it is about 22 GW of average demand.
A share of one country's use. Read it next to the whole, and never mix it with a global share.

parts:
.
Its main scenario, the Reference Case, puts

parts.note: A model's projection six years ahead, not a measurement: 2024 is the report's last historical year.
The authors' own range: its top is 1.6 times its bottom. The IEA's early-2025 projection, about 430 TWh, sits below it, as the report notes (p. 11).
Capacity, not energy: the report turns 649 TWh into GW by assuming connections are used at 50% on average.
What counts as a data center is a choice; a study that includes mining reports a larger number.

missing.note: Who pays for the new lines and plants that serve large loads depends on each utility's [[tariff|tariff]], its rules for what customers pay, and the story does not say. Analyst lesson [[lesson:a04-retail-tariffs|A4]] covers large-load tariffs.

envelope.q: 649 TWh in a year is how much power, on average?
feedback: That divides by 87.6 instead of 8.76: check the powers of ten.
Right: 649,000 GWh ÷ 8,760 h ≈ 74 GW, running all year.
TWh and GW are different kinds of unit: one is an amount, the other a rate.
That multiplies by the hours instead of dividing.

stories.take: I accept the direction, strong growth in U.S. data-center use by 2030, but not the exact 11.8%. A new estimate built on lower chip shipments or lower server power would change my mind. Confidence: medium, since credible projections still differ by about 50%.

sources.label: LBNL, United States Data Center Energy Usage Report: 2025 Update, pp. 5, 8–11 (PDF)

stories.headline: A record 15 GW of batteries joined the U.S. grid in 2025
stories.framing: Our paraphrase of how the data release was headlined.

parts.text: a record 15 GW of battery storage
parts.note: GW is power: how fast the batteries can deliver, not how much energy they hold. Energy in GWh needs the duration, which the story does not give.
Preliminary counts come from a monthly inventory and are revised when the final annual data arrive.

parts:
.
At the start of the year,

parts.note: Planned is not built: actual additions were about 82% of the amount first planned (15 ÷ 18.2).
A GW of solar makes less energy in a year than a GW of a plant that runs most hours. Compare capacity factors (average output ÷ rated power), not GW.
Big for one year. For scale, U.S. use averaged about 480 GW across 2025 (4.20 trillion kWh ÷ 8,760 h).

parts.text: The count covers utility-scale plants of 1 MW and up
parts.note: Home batteries and rooftop solar sit outside this count.

missing.note: Who pays for the batteries, and who earns from them, depends on market rules and contracts; the story does not say. Analyst lesson [[lesson:a02-contracts-risk|A2]] covers contracts and risk.

envelope.q: How much energy can 15 GW of batteries store?
options: It depends on how many hours they last
feedback: 15 GW alone does not give the energy: 15 GWh would mean the fleet averages one hour at full power, which the story does not say.
Only if they average exactly four hours; the story does not say.
Right: energy (GWh) = power (GW) × duration (h), and the duration is missing.

stories.take: I accept that a record amount of battery power, about 15 GW, came online in 2025, as a preliminary count. Final annual data showing a much lower figure would change my mind. Confidence: high for the power; the energy stored cannot be known from this story.

stories.intro: Two terms first: [[voltage|voltage]] is the electrical push on the lines. Supplying or absorbing [[reactive-power|reactive power]] helps keep local voltage within safe limits, neither too low nor too high.
stories.headline: Renewables caused the Iberian blackout
stories.framing: Our paraphrase of a claim that circulated soon after; no single outlet is quoted.
parts: At 12:33 CEST (11:33 in Portugal) on 28 April 2025,

parts.text: the continental power systems of Spain and Portugal
parts.note: The mainland grids of two countries went dark, not one plant or one city: that is why a formal investigation followed.

parts.text: Early posts and headlines named one cause
parts.note: The claim came before the evidence: the expert panel's factual report took 158 days, its final report 326.
A single cause from early, partial information. Ask who says it and what data they had.

parts:
.
The European grid operators' expert panel found

parts.note: Control rules, regulation practices and protection settings are part of the system, not only the power plants.

parts.text: gaps in voltage and reactive-power control
parts.note: Frequency responds to any gap between supply and demand (lesson 0). Voltage also depends on local network conditions and reactive-power control, so a yearly energy total cannot diagnose this blackout.

parts: , power swings (oscillations), and generators tripping off one after another (a cascade).

missing.q: Which question would test the headline's claim of a cause?
missing.note: Compared with what? The headline skips the test: would the same plants with different control settings, or different plants with the same settings, have held? The panel's event-by-event analysis is how such questions get answered.

envelope.q: How long after the blackout did the expert panel publish its final report?

stories.take: I reject the claim that renewables alone caused the blackout. An investigation tracing the collapse to one cause would change my mind. Confidence: high that there was no single cause, because the expert panel found many interacting factors.

spotter.text: The new battery can store 100 MW.
spotter.fix: Stored energy is in MWh; 100 MW is how fast it charges or discharges. A 100 MW, four-hour battery stores 400 MWh.

spotter.text: U.S. data centers used about 192 TWh of electricity in 2024.
spotter.fix: TWh over a year is an amount of energy: LBNL's estimate for 2024.

spotter.text: A 13 kWh home battery can run an average U.S. home for a month.
spotter.fix: An average home bought about 899 kWh a month (EIA, 2022 data), so 13 kWh lasts about 10 hours.

spotter.text: The plant's two 500 MW units will generate 1,000 MW every hour of the year.
spotter.fix: The ratings set the maximum power, not the output: plants run below nameplate and stop for maintenance, so a year's energy depends on hours and output. Average output ÷ nameplate is the capacity factor (lesson 5).

spotter.text: In 2025 the United States used about 4,200 TWh of electricity.
spotter.fix: 4.20 trillion kWh is 4,200 TWh (EIA, data for 2025).

spotter.text: A town of 10,000 homes needs about 10 GW of power.
spotter.fix: At EIA's 10,791 kWh a home a year (2022 data), 10,000 homes use about 108 GWh a year: about 12 MW on average. Even a peak a few times higher is far below 10 GW.

rungs.label: Operating
rungs.text: It runs and is counted as in service.

rungs.text: It delivers what it was built to deliver.

items.text: 15 GW of batteries entered service in 2025 (preliminary count)
items.note: Operating, as counted so far. Whether each battery delivers its rated hours is the next rung up.

items.text: 18.2 GW of batteries planned for 2025, as reported at the start of the year
items.note: Announced: a plan. Funding, permits and building each need their own evidence. Actual additions were about 82% of it.

items.text: 649 TWh of U.S. data-center use in 2030
items.note: Not on the ladder at all: a projection is a model's output, not a stage of anything being built.
